title: Bitcoin Script Playground — a stack machine you can step through
description: A teaching interpreter for a subset of Bitcoin Script. It runs an unlocking script and then a locking script one opcode at a time, animating the stack, marking skipped IF/ELSE branches and saying exactly why a spend fails. SHA-256 and RIPEMD-160 are written from scratch and checked against published test vectors on every load, and OP_CHECKSIG is a clearly labelled simulation.
prompt: Build a Bitcoin Script playground: a stack-machine interpreter for a teaching subset with data pushes, OP_DUP, OP_DROP, OP_SWAP, OP_ADD, OP_SUB, OP_EQUAL, OP_EQUALVERIFY, OP_VERIFY, OP_IF/OP_ELSE/OP_ENDIF, OP_SHA256 and OP_HASH160. Implement SHA-256 and RIPEMD-160 properly and prove them against known test vectors. OP_CHECKSIG should be a clearly labelled simulated check with no real ECDSA. Let me step through a script and watch the stack animate, with presets for a simulated P2PKH spend and a hash puzzle. It should feel like an engineer's notebook, not another dark crypto dashboard.

methodology: Known-answer tests: the page's own SHA-256 is checked against the FIPS 180-2 vectors (including the million-'a' message), RIPEMD-160 against the reference vectors from its designers (empty, 'a', 'abc', 'message digest', the alphabet, a million 'a'), and HASH160 against the BIP-173 generator-key example.
The hash implementations were also checked offline against Node's crypto module at the 55-, 56- and 64-byte padding boundaries before the page was written.

Step-level state checks for P2PKH: after each Step click the spec compares the stack to expected values (DUP gives [sig, pub, pub], HASH160 gives hash160(pub)), checks the program-counter chip on the tape, and checks that Step back restores the previous state exactly.

Negative paths, each checked for its exact error: the wrong key fails at step 6 (OP_EQUALVERIFY), a forged signature ends with false, a bad preimage leaves false, an unknown opcode is a parse error, and there are cases for an unbalanced IF across scripts, a missing ENDIF, stack underflow and OP_VERIFY on false.
Consensus details that are easy to get wrong: minimal script-number encoding (-1 → 81, 128 → 8000, -128 → 8080) and negative zero (0x80) counting as false.
risks: Bit-level mistakes in the hash functions (a wrong rotation table or endianness in the length padding); the self-test badge makes any regression visible to users as well as to tests.
IF/ELSE nesting inside a skipped branch must not flip on ELSE; the page tracks whether the outer branch was executing.
Step back relies on snapshots, so a shallow copy of any nested array would corrupt history.
Visitors could mistake the simulated CHECKSIG for real cryptography, so the page labels it in the note, the log and the opcode table.
qa.playwright: This page is deterministic and pure, so the spec leans on page.evaluate into window.__script for known-answer tests: hashing a million bytes and running whole scripts headlessly is fast and exact. The UI tests click Step and read both the rendered stack (data-testid stack-item counts and labels) and the interpreter state, so a rendering bug and a logic bug fail differently. The Run button animates with setInterval; with emulateMedia({ reducedMotion: 'reduce' }) the interval drops to 40 ms and Playwright's auto-waiting toHaveText covers the rest, so no fixed sleeps are needed. Visual snapshots were not used because the monospace wrapping of long hashes differs between desktop and Pixel 7.
coverage: SHA-256, RIPEMD-160 and HASH160 known-answer vectors; hash lab UI
Stepping the P2PKH spend with stack checks at each opcode; step back
Wrong-key failure at OP_EQUALVERIFY; forged signature
Hash puzzle with right and wrong preimages; parse errors
IF/ELSE skipping and the branch stack
Script-number encoding, negative zero, underflow and unbalanced branches

a11y: Every control is a native button or labelled textarea, and preset choices expose aria-pressed. The verdict is an aria-live status that names the failing step and reason. The stack is a labelled list whose items carry text labels (number, text, true/false, simulated key) as well as colour.
